Jose Marti. A Cuban poet, essayist, and revolutionary who wielded the pen as a weapon against Spanish colonialism and American imperialism, making literature and politics inseparable. Born in eighteen fifty-three, Marti would die fighting for Cuban freedom in eighteen ninety-five, embodying the Romantic ideal of the artist-activist and becoming a foundational symbol of Latin American identity and resistance.

His luminous, innovative verse helped define Spanish-American Modernism. His collection Ismaelillo, published in eighteen eighty-two, contained tender, playful poems dedicated to his son, introducing a more intimate and vulnerable Modernist voice into Spanish-language poetry. In eighteen ninety-one came Simple Verses, a collection of deceptively simple, aphoristic poems that became iconic in Cuban culture. The collection includes "My Verse," also known as "Cultivo una rosa blanca"—a statement of artistic independence.

Marti pioneered Spanish-American Modernism, a literary movement that rejected nineteenth-century realism in favour of musicality, innovation, and aesthetic experimentation, drawing on Symbolism and Parnassianism. Exiled from Cuba, he lived in New York, where he wrote prolifically as a journalist and essayist, earning a living while articulating his vision of Cuban independence and the responsibilities of the artist. His work became an influence on Ruben Dario and the broader Modernist movement, with his formal innovation and fusion of personal emotion with political conviction becoming a model for generations.

Marti died in eighteen ninety-five fighting for Cuban independence against Spain, and his death elevated his status from poet to martyr and revolutionary hero. He became the founding father of modern Cuban letters and of Cuban national consciousness, his life and legacy intimately bound up with the Cuban independence movement and his courageous sacrifice for the cause he articulated in his writing.
